notes:
1. Rural Welfare — Meaning and Scope

  • Rural welfare refers to government policies and programmes designed to improve the economic and social conditions of rural people.
  • It is broader than agricultural development because it includes employment, housing, roads, drinking water, sanitation, social protection, livelihoods, skills, credit, digital access and local infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agricultural Development → Mainly Farming

Rural Development → Farming + Livelihoods + Infrastructure + Welfare + Governance

2. Major Objectives of Rural Development

Rural welfare seeks to:

  • Reduce poverty and vulnerability.
  • Create employment.
  • Build sustainable livelihoods.
  • Improve housing.
  • Provide roads and connectivity.
  • Improve drinking water and sanitation.
  • Extend social protection.
  • Strengthen women's economic participation.
  • Improve skills, credit and market access.
  • Strengthen Panchayati Raj.
  • Reduce rural–urban disparities.

3. Evolution of Rural Development in India

The broad evolution can be understood as:

Community Development

→ Poverty Alleviation

→ Wage Employment and Asset Creation

→ Livelihood Missions

→ Integrated Rural Development

4. Community Development Programme — 1952

  • The Community Development Programme was launched in 1952.
  • It was among India's earliest organised rural-development initiatives after Independence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Community Development Programme → 1952

5. National Extension Service — 1953

  • The National Extension Service followed in 1953.
  • It extended development administration and technical guidance to rural areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Extension Service → 1953

6. Important Earlier Rural Programmes

Major programmes introduced over different periods included:

  • Integrated Rural Development Programme.
  • National Rural Employment Programme.
  • Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme.
  • Jawahar Rozgar Yojana.
  • Employment Assurance Scheme.
  • Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana.
  • Indira Awaas Yojana.
  • Many were later reorganised or replaced by broader rights-based or mission-mode programmes.

7. MGNREGA — Legal Employment Guarantee

  • MGNREGA refers to the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act.
  • The Act was enacted in 2005.
  • It provides a legal employment entitlement rather than merely an executive welfare benefit.
📌 Must-Memorise

MGNREGA Act → 2005

8. MGNREGA — 100-Day Guarantee

  • MGNREGA provides up to 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to a rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

100 Days → Per Rural Household

Not 100 Days Separately for Every Adult Member

9. MGNREGA — Demand-Driven Nature

  • MGNREGA is designed to be demand-driven.
  • Employment is linked to a statutory right to seek work under the Act.
📌 Must-Memorise

MGNREGA → Demand-Driven + Legally Backed

10. MGNREGA — Main Types of Works

MGNREGA works can include:

  • Water conservation.
  • Drought proofing.
  • Land development.
  • Irrigation.
  • Rural connectivity.
  • Soil conservation.
  • Natural-resource management.

11. MGNREGA — Wage Employment Plus Asset Creation

  • MGNREGA combines wage employment with creation of durable rural assets.
  • Farm ponds, water-harvesting structures, rural roads, irrigation works and land-development works are examples.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MGNREGA ≠ Mere Cash-Transfer Programme

12. MGNREGA — Job Card

  • Eligible rural households can register and obtain a Job Card.
  • It records household and employment-related information.
📌 Must-Memorise

MGNREGA → Job Card

13. Gram Panchayat — MGNREGA Role

Gram Panchayats play an important role in:

  • Registration.
  • Planning.
  • Work execution.
  • Monitoring.
  • Local implementation.

14. Social Audit — Meaning

  • A social audit allows the community to examine public records, expenditure, works and implementation.
  • It strengthens transparency and accountability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Social Audit → Community Examination of Public Programme

15. Gram Sabha — Social Audit Role

  • The Gram Sabha plays an important role in social audit and local accountability under rural-development programmes.

16. DAY-NRLM — Meaning

  • DAY-NRLM stands for Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana–National Rural Livelihoods Mission.
  • It seeks to reduce rural poverty through strong community institutions and sustainable livelihoods.
📌 Must-Memorise

DAY-NRLM → Rural Livelihoods + Community Institutions

17. DAY-NRLM — Women's SHG Focus

DAY-NRLM particularly promotes:

  • Women's Self-Help Groups.
  • Savings.
  • Bank linkage.
  • Formal credit.
  • Livelihood diversification.
  • Enterprise development.
  • Financial literacy.
  • Skills.
  • Market access.

18. MGNREGA vs DAY-NRLM

MGNREGA:

  • Primarily wage employment.
  • Demand-driven.
  • Backed by legislation.

DAY-NRLM:

  • Primarily livelihoods.
  • SHGs.
  • Credit.
  • Enterprise.
  • Skills.
  • Markets.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MGNREGA ≠ DAY-NRLM

19. Self-Help Group — SHG

  • An SHG is generally a small voluntary group whose members save regularly and undertake collective financial and livelihood activities.
  • Internal savings can support member lending.
  • Eligible groups can later access formal bank credit.
📌 Must-Memorise

SHG → Savings + Credit + Livelihoods + Empowerment

20. SHG–Bank Linkage

  • SHG–Bank Linkage connects organised groups with formal banking institutions.
  • It can reduce excessive dependence on informal moneylenders.

21. SHGs — Major Livelihood Activities

SHGs may engage in:

  • Dairy.
  • Food processing.
  • Tailoring.
  • Handicrafts.
  • Retail.
  • Small-scale production.
  • Farm-based enterprises.

22. SHGs — Women's Empowerment Role

SHGs can strengthen:

  • Financial literacy.
  • Women's leadership.
  • Household decision-making.
  • Awareness of schemes.
  • Community organisation.

23. DDU-GKY — Rural Skill Development

  • DDU-GKY stands for Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana.
  • It focuses on skill development linked with employment opportunities for eligible rural youth.
📌 Must-Memorise

DDU-GKY → Rural Youth Skill Development

24. DDU-GKY — Skill Areas

Training may cover areas such as:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
  • Retail.
  • Hospitality.
  • Technical skills.
  • Digital skills.
  • Services.

25. Rural Entrepreneurship

  • Rural self-employment and enterprise development can reduce dependence on seasonal agricultural work.
  • Successful enterprises require more than credit.

Important supports include:

  • Credit.
  • Skills.
  • Mentoring.
  • Market access.
  • Business support.

26. Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme

  • The Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme operates within the rural-livelihood framework.
  • It encourages rural enterprise development and local employment creation.

27. PMAY-G — Rural Housing

  • PMAY-G stands for Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana–Gramin.
  • It replaced the earlier Indira Awaas Yojana.
  • Its present form has been implemented from 2016–17.
📌 Must-Memorise

PMAY-G → Rural Housing

Present Form → 2016–17

28. PMAY-G — Objective

  • PMAY-G seeks to provide pucca houses with basic amenities to eligible rural households that are houseless or live in inadequate housing.

Housing contributes to:

  • Safety.
  • Health.
  • Dignity.
  • Household asset creation.
  • Protection from climate.
  • Better sanitation.

29. Housing Convergence

Better rural housing outcomes arise when housing is connected with:

House

  • Water
  • Toilet
  • Electricity
  • Connectivity
📌 Must-Memorise

Rural Housing → Convergence, Not House Alone

30. PMGSY — Rural Roads

  • PMGSY stands for Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana.
  • It was launched in December 2000.
  • Its original objective was all-weather road connectivity to eligible unconnected rural habitations.
📌 Must-Memorise

PMGSY → Rural Roads → December 2000

31. Rural Roads — Wider Benefits

Rural roads improve access to:

  • Markets.
  • Schools.
  • Hospitals.
  • Employment centres.
  • Government services.
  • Transport networks.

They also reduce the difficulty of moving farm inputs and produce.

32. PMAY-G vs PMGSY

  • PMAY-G → Rural housing.
  • PMGSY → Rural roads.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

PMAY-G ≠ PMGSY

33. NSAP — Social Assistance

  • NSAP stands for National Social Assistance Programme.
  • It provides social assistance to eligible vulnerable persons and households.
📌 Must-Memorise

NSAP → Social Assistance

34. Major NSAP Components

Important components include:

  • Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme.
  • Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme.
  • Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme.
  • National Family Benefit Scheme.
  • Annapurna Scheme.

35. NSAP vs MGNREGA

NSAP:

  • Social assistance.
  • Eligibility-based protection.

MGNREGA:

  • Wage payment in return for work.
  • Demand-driven employment guarantee.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Social Assistance ≠ Wage Employment

36. Social Assistance vs Social Insurance

Social assistance:

  • Financed mainly from public resources.
  • Provided according to eligibility.

Social insurance:

  • Generally linked with contributions from workers, employers or both.

37. SBM-G — Rural Sanitation

  • SBM-G stands for Swachh Bharat Mission–Grameen.
  • It was launched on 2 October 2014.
  • Its first phase focused strongly on sanitation coverage and elimination of open defecation.
📌 Must-Memorise

SBM-G → 2 October 2014

38. ODF — Open Defecation Free

  • ODF stands for Open Defecation Free.
  • SBM-G Phase I focused strongly on achieving and sustaining ODF outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

ODF → Open Defecation Free

39. SBM-G Phase II — ODF Plus

Phase II focuses on:

  • Sustaining ODF status.
  • Solid-waste management.
  • Liquid-waste management.
  • Plastic-waste management.
  • Greywater management.
  • Village cleanliness.
📌 Must-Memorise

Phase I → ODF

Phase II → ODF Plus

40. Sanitation — Behavioural Change

  • Toilet construction alone does not guarantee sanitation.
  • Proper usage, maintenance and behavioural change are also essential.

41. GOBARdhan

  • GOBARdhan promotes productive management of biodegradable rural waste.

Potential outputs include:

  • Biogas.
  • Bio-slurry.
  • Organic manure.
  • Waste-to-wealth products.
📌 Must-Memorise

GOBARdhan → Biodegradable Waste → Waste to Wealth

42. Jal Jeevan Mission — JJM

  • Jal Jeevan Mission was launched in 2019.
  • It seeks functional household tap-water connections for rural households.
📌 Must-Memorise

JJM → Rural Drinking Water → 2019

43. FHTC — Meaning

  • FHTC stands for Functional Household Tap Connection.
  • The objective is not merely installation of a tap.
  • Water should be adequate, regular and of prescribed quality.
📌 Must-Memorise

FHTC → Functional Household Tap Connection

44. JJM — Service-Level Norm

  • The rural service-level framework uses 55 litres per capita per day as an important planning norm.
📌 Must-Memorise

JJM Planning Norm → 55 Litres per Capita per Day

45. JJM — Source Sustainability

Water security also requires:

  • Rainwater harvesting.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Water conservation.
  • Greywater management.
  • Community participation.

46. SBM-G vs JJM

  • SBM-G → Rural sanitation and ODF/ODF Plus.
  • JJM → Functional rural drinking-water service.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SBM-G ≠ JJM

47. Mission Antyodaya

  • Mission Antyodaya is a convergence and monitoring initiative for rural development.
  • It assesses development gaps at the Gram Panchayat level.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mission Antyodaya → Convergence + Gram Panchayat Gap Assessment

48. Mission Antyodaya — Core Chain

Village Data

→ Identify Gaps

→ Set Local Priorities

→ Converge Schemes

→ Monitor Outcomes

49. Mission Antyodaya — Areas Assessed

It can examine gaps involving:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Livelihoods.
  • Agriculture.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Social development.
  • Financial inclusion.
  • Public services.

50. SAGY — Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana

  • SAGY was launched in 2014.
  • It promotes integrated development of selected Gram Panchayats with an important facilitating role for Members of Parliament.
📌 Must-Memorise

SAGY → 2014 → Model Village Development

51. SAGY — Development Areas

SAGY can focus on:

  • Sanitation.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Livelihoods.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Environment.
  • Social development.
  • Good governance.
  • Community participation.

52. SAGY — Funding Principle

  • SAGY emphasises convergence of existing schemes and local resources.
  • It is not simply a separate large financial entitlement for every village activity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SAGY ≠ One Separate Fund for Every Development Work

53. Mission Antyodaya vs SAGY

Mission Antyodaya:

  • Gap assessment.
  • Data-based Gram Panchayat planning.
  • Convergence monitoring.

SAGY:

  • Integrated development of selected Gram Panchayats.
  • MP facilitation.
  • Model-village approach.

54. Watershed Development — Meaning

  • A watershed is an area from which rainfall and surface water drain towards a common outlet.
  • Watershed development integrates management of soil, water, vegetation and natural resources.
📌 Must-Memorise

Watershed Development → Soil + Water + Vegetation + Livelihoods

55. Watershed Development — Importance

It is especially important in:

  • Rain-fed areas.
  • Drought-prone regions.

Its objectives include:

  • Soil conservation.
  • Rainwater conservation.
  • Erosion control.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Vegetation improvement.
  • Drought resilience.
  • Livelihood support.

56. Common Watershed Works

Examples include:

  • Check dams.
  • Contour bunding.
  • Farm ponds.
  • Percolation structures.
  • Drainage-line treatment.
  • Afforestation.
  • Soil-moisture conservation.

57. Watershed Development — Welfare Link

Better natural-resource management can improve:

  • Crop production.
  • Livestock activity.
  • Rural employment.
  • Drought resilience.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Watershed Development ≠ Irrigation Alone

58. BharatNet — Rural Digital Connectivity

  • BharatNet primarily strengthens rural broadband connectivity, especially to Gram Panchayats.
📌 Must-Memorise

BharatNet → Rural Broadband Connectivity

59. Common Service Centres — CSCs

  • CSCs provide assisted access to digital and public services.
  • They are especially useful where citizens lack devices, connectivity or digital skills.
📌 Must-Memorise

CSC → Assisted Digital Service Access

60. BharatNet vs CSC

  • BharatNet → Connectivity layer.
  • CSC → Assisted service-access layer.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

BharatNet ≠ CSC

61. Rural Digital Services

Digital access can support:

  • Government applications.
  • Certificates.
  • Banking.
  • Insurance.
  • Utility payments.
  • Digital literacy.
  • Telemedicine.
  • Education.
  • Grievance systems.

62. Digital Divide — Rural Welfare Challenge

Digitalisation can improve service delivery but may exclude citizens because of:

  • Weak connectivity.
  • Lack of devices.
  • Low digital literacy.
  • Language barriers.

Therefore rural digitalisation requires:

Connectivity + Devices + Skills + Assisted Access

63. Panchayati Raj — Constitutional Status

  • Panchayati Raj Institutions received constitutional status through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
📌 Must-Memorise

73rd Constitutional Amendment → Panchayati Raj Institutions

64. Gram Panchayat and Gram Sabha

Gram Panchayat:

  • Village-level local-government institution.

Gram Sabha:

  • Forum for direct local participation by village residents.

65. Panchayati Raj — Rural Development Role

Local institutions contribute to:

  • Planning.
  • Programme implementation.
  • Beneficiary identification.
  • Monitoring.
  • Social audit.
  • Maintenance of local assets.

66. Convergence — Meaning

  • Convergence means coordinating complementary programmes instead of implementing them in isolation.

A household may simultaneously require:

  • Employment.
  • Housing.
  • Roads.
  • Water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Credit.
  • Social assistance.
  • Digital access.
📌 Must-Memorise

Convergence → Multiple Schemes, One Development Outcome

67. Major Rural Scheme Mapping

  • MGNREGA → Employment + Assets.
  • DAY-NRLM → Livelihoods + SHGs.
  • PMAY-G → Housing.
  • PMGSY → Roads.
  • SBM-G → Sanitation.
  • JJM → Drinking water.
  • NSAP → Social assistance.
  • Mission Antyodaya → Gap assessment + convergence.
  • SAGY → Integrated model village.
  • Watershed programmes → Natural resources.
  • BharatNet / CSCs → Digital access.

68. Financial Inclusion — Meaning

Financial inclusion means expanding access to:

  • Bank accounts.
  • Savings.
  • Credit.
  • Insurance.
  • Pensions.
  • Digital payments.

69. Direct Benefit Transfer — DBT

  • DBT means transferring eligible government benefits directly through recognised financial channels.

Potential benefits include:

  • Faster transfer.
  • Reduced cash handling.
  • Better traceability.
  • Reduced duplication.
  • Better targeting.
📌 Must-Memorise

DBT → Benefit-Delivery Mechanism

70. DBT — Important Limitation

  • DBT depends on accurate beneficiary records, banking access, authentication, connectivity and digital literacy.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

DBT ≠ A Single Welfare Scheme

71. Business Correspondents

  • Business Correspondents extend basic banking services to areas without easily accessible bank branches.
  • They are important for last-mile financial inclusion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Business Correspondent → Last-Mile Banking Access

72. Tamil Nadu — Rural Development Architecture

  • Tamil Nadu implements both Union-supported programmes and State-specific rural-development schemes through its Rural Development and Panchayat Raj administrative system.

73. THAI — Tamil Nadu Village Habitations Improvement Scheme

  • THAI refers to the Tamil Nadu Village Habitations Improvement Scheme.
  • It was introduced from 2011–12.
  • A distinctive feature was its focus on the habitation as the unit for identifying infrastructure gaps.
📌 Must-Memorise

THAI → 2011–12 → Habitation-Level Infrastructure Approach

74. Why THAI Used the Habitation Approach

  • Different habitations within the same Village Panchayat can have very different infrastructure conditions.
  • The habitation-level approach helped identify more localised development gaps.

75. Anaithu Grama Anna Marumalarchi Thittam

  • Anaithu Grama Anna Marumalarchi Thittam is an important Tamil Nadu rural-development initiative.
  • It follows an integrated village-development approach to strengthen basic rural infrastructure according to identified local needs.
📌 Must-Memorise

AGAMT → Integrated Village Development

76. Tamil Nadu — Rural Roads

  • Tamil Nadu operates programmes to improve and maintain Village Panchayat and Panchayat Union roads.
  • Rural roads support access to markets, education, health care, employment and public services.

77. Tamil Nadu — Women's SHGs

  • Tamil Nadu has a strong history of women-led Self-Help Group development.
  • SHGs support savings, bank credit, livelihoods, leadership and community participation.

78. Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women

  • The Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women plays an important institutional role in women's SHG and livelihood programmes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women → Important SHG Institution

79. Tamil Nadu Rural Development — Core Mapping

  • THAI → Habitation-level infrastructure.
  • Anaithu Grama Anna Marumalarchi Thittam → Integrated village development.
  • Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women → SHGs and women's livelihoods.
  • Rural roads → Connectivity.
  • Local bodies → Implementation and monitoring.

80. Implementation Challenge — Beneficiary Identification

  • Eligible households may be excluded while ineligible households may sometimes be included.
  • Accurate and regularly updated records are therefore essential.

81. Implementation Challenge — Administrative Capacity

Effective delivery requires:

  • Trained personnel.
  • Adequate staffing.
  • Financial-management capacity.
  • Technology.
  • Strong local institutions.

82. Delayed Payments

  • Delayed wages, pensions or transfers reduce programme effectiveness.
  • Poor households with limited savings are particularly affected.

83. Awareness and Digital Exclusion

  • Citizens cannot claim benefits effectively without knowledge of eligibility and rights.
  • Digital systems can improve monitoring but may also create exclusion when connectivity or literacy is weak.

84. Asset Quality and Maintenance

  • Rural programmes should not be judged only by money spent.
  • Houses, roads, water systems, watershed structures and employment assets must be useful, durable and maintained.
📌 Must-Memorise

Expenditure ≠ Development Outcome

85. Fragmentation Across Departments

  • Separate implementation by multiple departments can create duplication and gaps.
  • Convergence initiatives seek to coordinate programmes around common local outcomes.

86. Accountability — Social Audit and Community Participation

Accountability improves through:

  • Social audits.
  • Public records.
  • Grievance systems.
  • Gram Sabha participation.
  • Community monitoring.
📌 Must-Memorise

Government Support + Local Government + Community Participation + Transparent Monitoring

87. Rural Welfare — Core Pillars

Modern rural welfare can be understood through:

  • Employment → MGNREGA.
  • Livelihoods → DAY-NRLM + SHGs + Skills.
  • Housing → PMAY-G.
  • Connectivity → PMGSY.
  • Water and sanitation → JJM + SBM-G.
  • Social protection → NSAP.
  • Integrated planning → Mission Antyodaya + SAGY.
  • Natural resources → Watershed development.
  • Digital access → BharatNet + CSCs + DBT.

  • 100 days do not apply separately to every adult member.
  • MGNREGA is demand-driven.
  • MGNREGA creates assets as well as employment.
  • Job Card is associated with MGNREGA.
  • Social audit involves community examination of implementation.
  • MGNREGA and DAY-NRLM are different.
  • DAY-NRLM focuses on livelihoods and community institutions.
  • SHGs combine savings, credit, livelihoods and empowerment.
  • DDU-GKY → Rural skills.
  • PMAY-G → Rural housing.
  • PMGSY → Rural roads.
  • PMGSY → December 2000.
  • PMAY-G present form → 2016–17.
  • NSAP → Social assistance.
  • NSAP is not an employment scheme.
  • SBM-G → Rural sanitation.
  • SBM-G launch → 2 October 2014.
  • ODF and ODF Plus are different.
  • JJM → Rural drinking water.
  • JJM launch → 2019.
  • FHTC means Functional Household Tap Connection.
  • Installing a tap alone does not guarantee functional water service.
  • JJM planning norm in source → 55 litres per capita per day.
  • GOBARdhan → Biodegradable waste management.
  • Mission Antyodaya → Gram Panchayat-level gap assessment and convergence.
  • SAGY → Integrated selected Gram Panchayat development with MP facilitation.
  • SAGY is not a separate fund for every project.
  • Watershed development is broader than irrigation.
  • BharatNet and CSCs are different.
  • BharatNet → Connectivity.
  • CSC → Assisted access.
  • DBT is a delivery mechanism, not a welfare scheme by itself.
  • Business Correspondents provide last-mile banking.
  • 73rd Constitutional Amendment → Panchayati Raj Institutions.

  • THAI is a Tamil Nadu programme.
  • THAI began from 2011–12.
  • THAI uses a habitation-level approach.
  • Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women is important for SHGs.
  • Expenditure alone does not guarantee effective rural development.
  • Convergence is a central principle of modern rural welfare.

97. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Rural development means? → Improvement of rural economic and social conditions through livelihoods, infrastructure, welfare and governance.
  • Rural development and agricultural development same? → No.
  • Community Development Programme launched? → 1952.
  • National Extension Service launched? → 1953.
  • MGNREGA Act year? → 2005.
  • MGNREGA provides? → Up to 100 days of wage employment per eligible rural household per financial year.
  • Is MGNREGA a legal entitlement? → Yes.
  • MGNREGA demand-driven? → Yes.
  • MGNREGA work nature? → Unskilled manual work with rural asset creation.
